{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Albert Baernstein II''' (25 April 1941,  [[Birmingham, Alabama]] – 10 June 2014, [[University City, Missouri]]) was an American mathematician.<ref>{{cite web|title=Obituary: Albert Baernstein, professor emeritus of mathematics, 73|url=https://source.washu.edu/2014/06/obituary-albert-baernstein-professor-emeritus-of-mathematics-73/|publisher=Washington University in St. Louis|date=16 June 2014}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Baernstein matriculated at the [[University of Alabama]], but after a year there he transferred to  [[Cornell University]], where he received his bachelor's degree in 1962. After working for a year for an insurance company, he became a graduate student in mathematics at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]], where he received his master's degree in 1964 and Ph.D. in 1968.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=9438}}</ref>

Baernstein was from 1968 to 1972 an assistant professor at [[Syracuse University]] and from 1972 to 2011 a professor at [[Washington University in St. Louis]], where he retired as professor emeritus.<ref name=Obit>{{cite journal|author=Drasin, David|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201507/rnoti-p815.pdf|title=Albert Baernstein II, 1941–2014|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|volume=62|year=2015|number=7|pages=815–818|doi=10.1090/noti1265|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Contributions==
The main focus of Baernstein's was analysis, especially [[complex analysis|function theory]] and symmetrization problems. His most important contribution is now called the Baernstein star-function. He originally introduced the star-function to solve an extremal problem posed by [[Albert Edrei]] in [[Nevanlinna theory]]. Later, the star-function was applied by Baernstein and others to several different extremal problems.<ref name=Obit/>

In 1978 he was an Invited Speaker with talk ''How the *-function solves extremal problems'' at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in [[Helsinki]].<ref>Baernstein II, Albert. "How the ∗-function solves extremal problems." Proc. Intern. Congr. Math.(Helsinki 1978) vol. 2 (1980): 638–644</ref> He supervised 15 doctoral students,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.stlouiscremation.com/obituary/albert-baernstein-ii|title=Albert Baernstein II|website=St. Louis Cremation|date=10 June 2014 }}</ref> including [[Juan J. Manfredi]].
